strengths: Synth-SBDH addresses a concrete clinical NLP resource gap with 8,767 synthetic examples covering 14 SBDH categories and pain, including spans, presence, temporality, and rationales. The public resource and demonstrated downstream utility support a Findings recommendation.

Classification gains on real clinical data are substantial. Prompt-based RoBERTa improves macro-F from 55.64 to 91.11 on MIMIC-SBDH-aligned, while standard RoBERTa improves from 72.38 to 80.71 on VA-SBDH. These results provide meaningful evidence that synthetic pretraining can benefit small clinical classifiers.

The experiments include multiple model families, three independent runs, exact and relaxed NER evaluation, and an informative low-resource analysis. Appendix D.2 also provides a useful comparison against real-data pretraining with approximately matched training steps.

Expert review of the entire 1,755-example synthetic test split is a substantial strength. The paper transparently reports corrections, omissions, and qualitative failure cases, and documents the generation prompt, 45 seed examples, model version, filtering procedure, annotation guidelines, and training configurations.
weaknesses: The claims of consistent improvement and broad generalizability exceed the results. Tables 4, 13, and 14 show negligible or negative gains for several encoder NER, Mamba, and Llama settings. The large T5 NER improvement primarily stabilizes a highly variable baseline. Both clinical evaluations include supervised target-domain fine-tuning, so the evidence establishes benefits under that adaptation setting, with substantial dependence on model and task.

The most dramatic rare-category result concerns only 18 housing-insecurity test positives. Variation across three training runs does not capture uncertainty from this small test sample. Confidence intervals over test examples and comparisons against class rebalancing and additional target-data training would strengthen the practical interpretation of these gains.

The rationale-distillation claim is only weakly supported. DSS improves macro-F by 0.66 points for T5 and 0.58 for FLAN-T5, with the latter nonsignificant at the reported p=0.36, and evaluation is confined to synthetic text. This demonstrates limited evidence for auxiliary rationale supervision, without establishing transferred reasoning capability. Real clinical extraction could be evaluated without requiring gold rationales at test time.

The annotation-quality metrics require clearer interpretation. The 71.06% figure is 2,478 kept annotations divided by 3,487 entries including additions; the 90.78% LLM evaluation excludes missing annotations and therefore uses a different basis. Appendix E.2 also accepts an existing GPT-4 category while requiring a more specific category for newly added annotations, making labels partly dependent on the original prediction. Standard extraction precision/recall and clearer agreement calculations would strengthen confidence in the benchmark.

Coverage of realistic clinical complexity remains limited: synthetic examples average 13.7 words, versus 35.13 and 47.43 in the clinical datasets. Experiments retain only presence-positive annotations and do not separately evaluate temporal prediction, leaving the utility of these advertised annotation dimensions unestablished.

Reproducibility is supported by extensive documentation but needs tighter reporting. The stated synthetic split sizes sum to 8,727 rather than 8,767, and annotation totals differ between Tables 2 and 10. Prompt-based classification templates and the significance-testing procedure are insufficiently specified. VA-SBDH's private status also limits independent reproduction of the NER and low-resource findings.
